newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican '97 cocoa output seen fit for Aztec kings.
newsitem.headline: Mexican '97 cocoa output seen fit for Aztec kings.

text.p: Mexican cocoa, a favorite food and a commodity-based currency of the former Aztec empire, is seen making a production comeback this year.

Cocoa farmers and government agriculture officials estimated this 1996-1997 harvest will be above average and well above the previous cycle that was dogged by inclement weather and financial doldrums.
But forecasts differ for the output expected from the current campaign.

Mexico's cocoa production swings traditionally between around 30,000 tonnes in poor cycles and 47,000 tonnes in good ones, according to trade and government sources. The Agriculture Ministry does not publish cocoa output data regularly.
The president of the National Association of Cocoa Producers estimated that Mexico's 1996-97 harvest will end between 50,000 and 55,000 tonnes - a record.

Laurence Rodriguez Torruco told Reuters his estimates were based on the production to date of 36,000 tonnes in the cycle's March-October harvesting period and on favorable weather conditions, with sufficient rain and hot spells.
Other cocoa farmers have also renegotiated burdensome debts which has also spurred them to invest in fertilisers this cycle that also should boost the crop and final production, he added.
Jorge Lara, deputy delegate for the Agriculture Ministry in Tabasco state, estimated Tabasco would produce more than 30,000 tonnes this 96-97 cycle.
"It (the state harvest) will probably reach 32,000 tonnes, giving a national harvest in the region of 40,000 tonnes," Lara predicted.
Traditionally, around 80 percent of the national crop is grown in the sultry southern state of Tabasco and almost all the remainder in the neighboring state of Chiapas.

In 95-96, Mexico's cocoa crop was one of the lowest recorded, hit by damage and fallout from Hurricanes Roxanne and Opal. Lara estimated the 95-96 national output was around 30,000 tonnes, with 24,000 tonnes coming from Tabasco.

Lara's forecast for this cycle would make the Tabasco harvest close to the 37,700 tonnes produced in the state in 1994-1995. That translated into a national harvest in the region of 47,000 tonnes -- one of the highest in recent history.

Cocoa was widely consumed by Aztec indians and is still a popular drink and even used in certain foods. One traditional dish called "mole" combines cocoa and hot chile peppers. Cocoa was used so widely that it was also traded as a currency in pre-Colombian markets.

Mexico no longer ranks among the world's top producer nations. Rodriguez Torruco admitted growers focus on supplying cocoa for the national market. Mexico does also export small volumes of beans, however.
The main national buyers are Compania Nestle, the Mexican unit of Swiss-based Nestle, and Empresas La Corona, a unit of Mexican food firm Grupo Corvi.
